claims.text: The dynamic strength–ductility balance of as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by interactions between partial-dislocation slip and stacking-fault formation.
The governing interaction between partial dislocations and stacking faults depends on temperature and strain rate.
Removing Co from FeNiCrMn lowers the stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes stacking-fault nucleation in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Stacking faults impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength or yield strength.
Stacking faults provide sites for localized plasticity and thereby preserve ductility.
Temperature and strain rate modulate stacking-fault formation and dislocation mobility.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates will produce a higher stacking-fault density in as-solidified FeNiCrMn.
Higher stacking-fault density will correlate with increased yield strength.
FeNiCrMn will retain sufficient ductility under the lower-temperature and higher-strain-rate conditions that increase stacking-fault density.
If stacking-fault activity is diminished, the expected strain hardening and strength enhancement will not occur.
Quasi-static loading is expected to have a smaller effect on stacking-fault formation than dynamic loading at comparable temperatures.
Significant post-solidification annealing, precipitation, or compositional variation may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Twinning and phase transformation are plausible competing dynamic-deformation mechanisms.
A dominant mechanism other than stacking-fault and partial-dislocation interactions would falsify the claim that those interactions primarily govern the dynamic response.

contradictions.description: The intervention and falsification design label the entire 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 range as dynamic loading, while the baseline separately calls for quasi-static tests; 10^-3 s^-1 is conventionally a quasi-static regime and therefore overlaps the stated intervention range, leaving the dynamic-versus-baseline comparison internally ambiguous.
